description: We are a group of web developers and 3D designers and space fans. We came together to use our coding and design abilities to create websites that're easy to use. By adding 3D graphics to design we work as a team to turn complicated information into fun and interactive online experiences. We enjoy using technology to make big ideas real.
summary:
What we developed
“Forgotten Equipment on Mars and the Moon” is an interactive 3D website that tells the stories of spacecraft and tools that humanity left behind on other worlds. Visitors choose Mars or the Moon, then fly into a rotating globe built from real photographs. Glowing markers on the globe lead to 14 pieces of equipment, such as Eagle’s descent stage, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, the Surveyor landers, Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity.

How it addresses the challenge
The challenge asks for storytelling about NASA’s discarded equipment. Instead of a list of facts, we turned each object into a short story: when it was used, what it did, and where it rests today. Placing the objects on a globe at their real latitude and longitude shows how far apart these places are and how much we have left behind. Each story is only five sentences, so people can read it quickly and keep exploring.

Why it is important
This equipment is part of humanity’s history on other worlds. It also shows the human side of exploration: Opportunity’s last message during the dust storm, Sojourner’s short life, and Apollo’s discarded descent stages. Telling these stories in a visual, interactive form makes them easier for students and the public to remember..

Built with
Three.js (3D globes, lighting and the atmosphere effect), GSAP (camera flights and animations), and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
details:
What the project does

This is an interactive 3D website that shows the spacecraft, rovers and landers humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars. The visitor starts on a black-and-blue landing page and chooses between two worlds, each shown with a real photo. After choosing, they get a 3D globe of that world that they can spin, tilt and zoom, much like Google Earth. Glowing markers on the globe show where each piece of equipment still sits. Clicking a marker, or a name in the side list, turns the globe to that spot and opens a card with a real photo, the year of the mission, its coordinates, its status (abandoned, dead, dormant, crashed or retired), a short story, and a link to more photos in NASA’s image library.

The site covers 18 sites, 9 on each world. On the Moon these include Apollo 11, the Apollo 15 and 17 rovers, Surveyor 3, Lunokhod 1, Chang’e 4, Chandrayaan-3, Luna 2 and Beresheet. On Mars they include Spirit, Opportunity, Viking 1, Pathfinder, Phoenix, Ingenuity, Beagle 2, Schiaparelli and Mars 3.

How it works
Landing page: the Moon and Mars photos are loaded live from Wikipedia. A soft blue glow follows the mouse across the page, and each card has its own spotlight that follows the cursor.
3D globe: a sphere is wrapped in a real surface map of the chosen planet, with a second map that adds relief so craters and ridges catch the light. A directional light gives a day and night side, and a thin shader-made atmosphere glow surrounds the planet (orange for Mars, pale blue for the Moon).
Controls: dragging rotates the globe with momentum, scrolling or pinching zooms, and the globe slowly spins when idle. Rotation uses quaternions, so the globe never flips or locks at the poles.
Markers: each site’s latitude and longitude is converted into a 3D position on the sphere. Clicking a marker casts a ray from the mouse into the scene to find which marker was hit. The globe then smoothly turns and zooms to bring that site to the center.
Photos: when a site is selected, the page asks the Wikipedia summary API for that article’s lead image and shows it in the info card. If no photo is found, it says so instead of breaking.
Benefits
It makes space history easier to explore than a plain list or table, because people can see where things are.
It is educational: it shows that space missions leave real objects on other worlds, and it raises topics like space debris and planetary protection.
It runs in any modern browser with nothing to install, on desktop, tablet or phone.
It is easy to extend: a new site is one extra line of data.
Goals
Make the history of lunar and Mars exploration visual and interactive.
Give users a Google-Earth-style way to browse another world.
Use real maps and real photographs, not drawings, so it feels authentic.
Keep it fast and lightweight, with a single file and no backend.
Tools, languages and technology
Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
3D library: Three.js (r128), loaded from the cdnjs content delivery network. It provides WebGL rendering, lighting, bump mapping, raycasting and custom shaders (GLSL) for the atmosphere.
Planet maps: real Moon and Mars surface and relief maps from the threex.planets collection (textures by James Hastings-Trew, Planet Pixel Emporium), loaded through jsDelivr and GitHub.
Photos and data: the Wikipedia REST API for the equipment photos, and the NASA Image Library for the “more photos” links.
Development: the project was built with the help of Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) and tested in Google Chrome.
Hardware and software requirements
Hardware: any computer, tablet or phone with a GPU that supports WebGL. No special hardware is needed.
Software: a modern web browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari or Brave.
Network: an internet connection is needed, because the 3D library, planet maps and photos are loaded online.
Limitations and future work
Site positions are approximate, based on published landing coordinates.
Photos depend on what Wikipedia shows for each article, and some may not be a picture of the exact object.
The maps are 1K resolution, so a very close zoom looks soft. Higher-resolution NASA maps could be added.
Future ideas include adding more sites (such as Soviet and Chinese missions and the Mars rovers still active), a timeline slider by year, and a search box.
